title: Procter & Gamble Q1 Earnings Beat Estimates on 4% Sales Growth; Sales Outlook Raised
excerpt: Core EPS of $2.00 topped the $1.89 consensus as net sales rose 4% to $23.28 billion; P&G raised its fiscal 2027 all-in sales growth outlook to 2–4% while holding EPS guidance.
body:
• Procter & Gamble's fiscal first-quarter core EPS of $2.00 beat the $1.89 consensus, as net sales rose 4% to $23.28 billion and organic sales grew 4% — about double the rate analysts expected.
  • All five segments beat organic sales estimates, led by Beauty (up 5.4% organically), Fabric & Home Care (4.8%) and Grooming (4.5%).
  • Core gross margin fell 160 basis points to 49.8%, and P&G raised its expected fiscal 2027 commodity cost hit to about $1.4 billion after tax, from $1.0 billion.
  • The company held its core EPS guidance at $6.89–$7.11 but raised its all-in fiscal 2027 sales growth outlook to 2–4%, reflecting the Thorne acquisition.

Procter & Gamble opened its fiscal 2027 with a cleaner beat than Wall Street expected, reporting first-quarter results on Thursday in which volume growth and favorable product mix drove sales about twice as fast as analysts had forecast. The shares rose 3.3% following the release.

Core earnings per share were $2.00, up 1% year over year and ahead of the $1.89 consensus estimate, according to Zacks and MarketBeat; diluted net EPS rose 1% to $1.97. Net sales increased 4% to $23.28 billion, beating consensus of roughly $22.8 billion. Organic sales also grew 4%, built from 2.4 points of volume growth, 1.1 points of favorable mix and 0.4 points of pricing, with foreign exchange neutral — well above the roughly 2% organic growth analysts had penciled in. Operating cash flow was $5.8 billion, free cash flow $4.4 billion, and the company returned $3.9 billion to shareholders through $2.6 billion of dividends and $1.3 billion of buybacks.

Every Segment Beat

The breadth was the story. Fabric & Home Care, the largest segment, grew sales 4% to $8.21 billion with organic growth of 4.8% on a 4.3% volume increase. Beauty sales rose 6% to $4.41 billion, with organic growth of 5.4% against a consensus near 3.6%, helped by higher volumes, favorable mix and currency gains. Grooming sales grew 4% to $1.89 billion and 4.5% organically — far ahead of the 0.7% forecast — while Baby, Feminine & Family Care sales rose 3% to $5.32 billion (3.0% organic) and Health Care sales rose 3% to $3.32 billion (2.7% organic), despite a 2.9% volume decline in health care that pricing and mix more than offset. All six regions and all 10 product categories posted organic growth, Greater China organic sales rose 8%, and 29 of the top 50 category-country combinations held or gained share.

Margins Squeezed, Cost Warning Raised

The offset was profitability. Core gross margin fell 160 basis points year over year to 49.8%, and core operating margin narrowed 80 basis points to 25.9%, as commodity, freight and energy costs outran productivity savings. Management now expects commodity costs to cut fiscal 2027 after-tax profit by about $1.4 billion, up from the $1.0 billion estimated previously. Chief Executive Shailesh Jejurikar said the quarter reflected sharpened execution of the company's integrated strategy and a strong start that keeps P&G on track despite geopolitical and economic challenges.

Guidance: Sales Up, EPS Held

For fiscal 2027, P&G maintained its core EPS guidance range of $6.89–$7.11 (flat to up 3%) and its organic sales growth outlook of 1–3%, but raised all-in net sales growth guidance to 2–4% from its prior range, citing the Thorne health-products acquisition that became effective October 1. Management expects roughly 3% organic growth in the first half with potential acceleration later in the year, while cautioning that consumer demand, oil prices, currencies and geopolitics could make individual quarters volatile. For Indian-American readers, the company is a familiar name at two levels: India-born Jejurikar now runs the world's largest consumer-goods maker, and its brands — Tide, Pampers, Gillette, Pantene and Oral-B — sit in most diaspora households' cabinets.
